newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FOCUS-Russia sees resumption of IMF loans soon.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Russia sees resumption of IMF loans soon.

text.p: Russia has completed work on a 1997 economic programme with the International Monetary Fund and the fund will probably agree to resume paying out money from its delayed $10 billion loan to Russia next month, the head of the central bank said on Friday.

But Central Bank Chairman Sergei Dubinin told a briefing that the IMF, which would start monitoring the Russian economy on a quarterly rather than monthly basis, would in future disburse funds at a slower rate than it had done last year.
Dubinin said he expected the IMF's board of directors to meet by mid-May to approve the 1997 part of the economic programme backed by the three-year Extended Fund Facility loan.
It would then agree to pay 500 million Special Drawing Rights (SDRs), about $685 million, for the first quarter of this year, and pay out money every quarter after that, he said.
"We expect the Board of Directors to take a decision in the first half of May, or at least by mid-May," Dubinin said.

"This depends on when our documents arrive and how long it takes to examine these documents and the mission's report, and after that we will apparently receive all the tranches for the first quarter in a volume of 500 million SDR, and after that similar tranches will be received on a quarterly basis."

Dubinin's comments echoed those of IMF Managing Director Michel Camdessus, who said in Washington on Thursday that he expected the board to approve the 1997 programme next month and start disbursing funds immediately afterwards.

Earlier this month Camdessus said the IMF would not release the 1997 money until the government submitted a new tax code to parliament. Russian businesses and foreign investors say the present tax system is arbitary, illogical and contradictory.

The fund was paying Russia monthly tranches of about $350 million last year. But Russian officials said the three-year loan was designed to pay out money at a faster rate in the first year, when it was most needed.
The IMF repeatedly delayed payments last year, and has disbursed nothing so far this year, as it is concerned at the low level of tax receipts, running far below budgeted levels.
The low revenues mean the government, which already owes trillions of roubles in unpaid wages and pensions, must either slash spending further or allow the budget deficit to widen.
That would either re-ignite inflation or stifle the economic recovery which is just starting after seven years of recession -- undermining the twin goals of the IMF programme.
The Russian government discussed on Friday plans to cut spending because of the first quarter shortfall, and put the final stages to the new tax code.
The IMF forecasts Russia's economy will at last start to grow this year, with gross domestic product rising 2.8 percent, while inflation will slow to a post-reform low of 14 percent.

Although the IMF has not paid Russia any money this year, the shift to quarterly monitoring and disbursements would allow both the Russian authorities and the fund to argue that payments have not been delayed in 1997.
With quarterly monitoring it would be quite normal to have a mission visit in April and a board decision in May.
Russian officials have in any case recently played down the importance of the IMF credits.
"Today the IMF loans do not play even a fifth of the role for Russia which they played two years ago," economic policy chief Anatoly Chubais said on Thursday.
Chubais, who is also Finance Minister, noted that Russia could now borrow money easily and almost as cheapily on the international capital market as it could from the IMF.
Russia, which successfully issued two jumbo Eurobonds in November and March, plans to tap the markets again in the next few months.
But the Russian authorities agree with the IMF that the tax question is crucial.

The State Tax Service says first quarter revenues were only 69 percent of budgeted levels, and Chubais and other ministers say the fiscal crisis is so grave that the very viability of the Russian state is questioned.
